content:
The constructors of docs#IO.Error all take an osCode : UInt32, however the semantics are rather confusing:

  • If the IO function producing the error uses native OS calls, then on unix it returns errno (eg ENOENT = 2), a signed int that is fortunately always positive.
  • If the IO function producing the error uses libuv, then it returns a UV error (eg UV_ENOENT = -2). This ends up mapped to UInt32.max - 2.

This means that swapping out the implementation of a runtime IO function (in a lean upgrade) to use libuv internally not only potentially breaks existing users, but also presents new users with confusingly wrapped-around error codes.

Should the lean_decode_uv_error flip the sign on its arguments to make them look like errno? Or is the thought that osCode is completely an implementation detail?
(if the latter, should lean4#14423 just update the expected values in the tests?)
I wonder whether we should just not report the osCode. Do you know of a case where the osCode is useful to have?

Given that the error codes differ on Linux and Windows (and are a libuv implementation detail anyway) and that we don't provide a way of matching an error number against the libuv error constants, surely it's not possible to do anything useful with them.

Eric Wieser said:

Should the lean_decode_uv_error flip the sign on its arguments to make them look like errno?

I think this would be a good change to make in your PR. The result won't really mean anything on Windows, but we can address that later.
Updated in the PR, thanks for the feedback

If the IO.Error changes in the future, it could be a good idea to take a look at Rust IO Error.

Rust has an internal ErrorData that holds the error (os, custom, simple, message), for the os ones it uses a RawOsError and a mapping to an ErrorKind for each system code via decode_error_kind for each sub system (windows, linux, and a lot more).
This would complexify IO.Error implementation, but would allow for better system mapping for different sub systems.

Julia Markus Himmel said:

I wonder whether we should just not report the osCode. Do you know of a case where the osCode is useful to have?

The Lean-to-Python FFI will use it to translate Lean errors to Python OSError exceptions. It could fix the error codes for each IO.Error constructor, though that may be slightly confusing for the Python side (and require reversing Lean's mapping per platform).
@Mac Malone after lean4#14479, the osCode value will always contain our best guess at an errno value on all platforms, so you should have an easy time constructing a Python OSError from that.
